title: Polymarked: Imporving physical density estimation with prediction markets
authors: David Siang-Li Jheng;Owen Chaffard;Andrei-Theodor Ginavar;Stefan Gaman;Rahul Tak
summary:
Using data from Polymarket's prediction markets on BTC prices and maturity matched Deribit BTC options, we evaluate whether prediction markets contain information relevant to physical density estimation beyond that of historical returns and traditional options. 

First results compare Deribit derivatives with prediction markets observed through the derivatives lens (a market in Polymarket is a Digital call option). Evidence of volatility smiles at short time to maturity is highlighted in both markets, while polymarket's smile tends to be more symmetric (no smirk). This is further supported by calibration analysis showing prediction markets to be better calibrated ( beat both historical methods and Deribit on Brier/log score). Mincer-Zarnowitz regression does highligh longshot bias expected in betting situations.
collaboration_needs: Contribute to modeling, providing reliable/strong benchmarks for physical density estimation.

title: Hierarchical Morphology Search
summary: We seek to extend the current framework for hierarchical/grouped time series forecasting and linear reconciliation. We highlight using the proof of the MinTrace optimal projection that aggregates serve as additional noisy observations of the bottom nodes' errors. Thus aggregate forecasts are only useful if their disagreement with bottom forecasts are informative of bottom errors, more than they cost in estimation (additional bias/variance). Using this theoretical framework we build a hierarchy search algorithm using greedy additions, we detail its benefit in different data regimes, including abstention in common benchmark datasets where no aggregates provides significant performance improvement.

title: Scaling Tabular Foundation Models for Credit Scoring
summary: Typical datasets in credit scoring applications can reach several hundred thousands to million rows. In this setting, tabular foundation models have been shown to fall off and not conserve their advantage over simpler ML methods. In order to scale these models to datasets several factors larger than their pretraining, we implement and benchmarks several methods to effectively retrieve local context for each test row or cluster while balancing bias and variance.

title: Resolving the Duplicate-Feature Paradox with ReSHAP: A Redundancy-Weighted Generalization of Shapley Attribution
authors: Adam Kurpisz, Jens Reil, Lucia T. Gomez, Branka H. Misheva
summary:
Shapley-value–based feature attribution methods are widely used to explain machine learning model predictions. However, when features are duplicated or highly correlated, their total attribution can be unfairly inflated, diminishing the attribution assigned to other important features. This paradox arises because traditional Shapley-based methods allocate joint contributions equally across all participating features, regardless of redundancy or informational overlap.

In this work, we propose ReSHAP, a redundancy-aware generalization of Shapley attribution that systematically resolves the attribution consequences of the duplicate-feature paradox. ReSHAP adjusts the allocation of credit within feature coalitions by down-weighting features that contribute redundant information. We begin by proving that no existing attribution method can simultaneously satisfy equal division and redundancy-invariance, even in instances without redundant features. This reveals a fundamental trade-off in designing fair attribution methods. Building on this insight, ReSHAP redefines how Shapley values are computed by redistributing interaction terms across feature subsets using a recursive weighting scheme, using only the standard value function without additional distributional assumptions. We support our theoretical findings with illustrative examples and experiments, highlighting the practical effectiveness of ReSHAP.

title: Applications of Interpretable and Explainable Machine Learning in Insurance Pricing
authors: Jens Reil, Axel Pison, Marcos R. Machado
subjects: Insurance pricing; Non-life; Explainable AI; XAI; SHAP; LIME; Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning
summary: This paper examines the application of interpretable and explainable machine learning (ML) to motor-insurance claim frequency and severity modeling, using generalized linear models (GLMs) as actuarial benchmarks. LightGBM, XGBoost, and a multi-layer perceptron are compared with Poisson and Gamma GLMs on data from a Dutch insurer. The study reports predictive-error measures and illustrates model behavior using SHAP and LIME, complemented by semi-structured interviews with five insurance professionals. The observed performance differences are small and depend on the model and metric: the MLP attains a lower mean absolute error than the GLM for both tasks but a slightly higher root mean squared error for claim frequency. The explanation analyses illustrate model-specific feature contributions, while the interviews identify transparency, validation, and governance concerns relevant to practical adoption. The study provides a case-based comparison of actuarial and ML methods and highlights the additional validation required before their operational use in insurance pricing.

title: Evaluating Explainable Artificial Intelligence Methods for Financial Time Series Forecasting
authors: Jens Reil, Branka H. Misheva, Lucia T. Gomez, Adam Kurpisz, Laura Spierdijk
subjects: Forecasting; Explainable AI; XAI; Volatility; Financial market; Stock market; Stylized facts
summary: This paper investigates the reliability of existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods in financial time series forecasting, with a particular focus on stock market volatility. Using a controlled experimental framework based on synthetic time series, the study examines how financial characteristics such as volatility clustering, heavy tails, temporal dependence, and structural regime changes affect the accuracy, stability, and faithfulness of explanations generated by commonly used XAI methods, including SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients. By incorporating established volatility forecasting approaches and progressively introducing realistic financial complexities, the study aims to distinguish model predictive performance from explanation quality. The framework is planned to subsequently be extended to real financial data.

title: Can Large Language Models Construct Risk-Appropriate and Efficient Portfolios?
authors: Jens Reil; Mohamed Faid; Julius Kooistra
subjects: Large Language Models; LLM; Stock Market; Investing; Digital Finance
summary: This paper investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct investment portfolios that align with individual investor risk preferences while maintaining financial efficiency. The study evaluates portfolio recommendations generated by multiple LLMs across different investor risk profiles. The recommended portfolios are assessed against the theoretical efficient frontier derived from Modern Portfolio Theory, examining their risk-return characteristics, diversification, and efficiency. By incorporating quantitative measures of portfolio efficiency, risk alignment, and utility regret, the study aims to distinguish between an LLM's ability to understand investor preferences and its ability to construct financially efficient portfolios. Ultimately, the paper seeks to evaluate the reliability and limitations of LLM-generated investment advice.

title: Developing a Scale of Public Explanation Needs for AI-Assisted Financial Applications
authors: Patri ia Marcella Evite; Maria Iannario
summary: To the best of our knowledge, there is limited psychometric evidence concerning information needs in a questionnaire for eliciting XAI requirements. It consequently remains unclear whether preferences for different categories of explanation content reflect a general explanation-needs construct, several related dimensions, or a profile of distinct information requirements. The present study addresses this gap by developing and psychometrically evaluating a scale of public explanation needs using survey responses from 503 responses with Item Response Theory (IRT).

title: Reciprocity Propensity Scores: An ML-based Framework for Non-monetary Economies
authors: Patricia Marcella Evite; Doina Bucur; Owen Chaffard; Will Ruddick
subjects: blockchain, explainable ai, forecasting, community vouchers
summary:
The paper's goal is two-fold. First, we aim to create a baseline reference for so-called perfect balance in reciprocal relationships, where we trace a person's activity from the transactions whether they have both given and received help from another user. In monetary transactions, this can be akin to a loan repayment. Second, based on the first objective's result, we will predict the users who are likely to reciprocate. To get the most accurate results, we will compare the performance of a suite of inherently interpretable and blackbox models. In the case of the latter, an explainable AI (XAI) is added to create an actionable result for the user and our partner NGO Grassroots Economics, accordingly. 

Our contribution is a quantitative complement to evaluation systems for financial credit in humanitarian contexts answering multiple calls for research such as Aiken et al. (2022).
